summary: Describes a periodic sampling method and metrics for assessing IP network performance, and argues for it as an alternative to the Poisson sampling in RFC 2330. Periodic streams suit measuring traffic that resembles constant bit rate flows such as voice, and apply to both active and passive measurements.

eli5.summary: To check how a road is doing, send cars at steady, evenly spaced times rather than at random. This note explains why that is useful and how to measure delay and loss this way.

questions: what is a periodic stream in network measurement
how to measure one way delay
why use periodic sampling instead of poisson
subtitle: Send packets at steady, evenly spaced times to measure the delay and loss that real-time media would see.

tldr.problem: Voice and video send equally sized packets at regular intervals, but the standard Poisson (random-timing) sampling of RFC 2330 does not mimic that pattern and samples only part of the network's behaviour.
tldr.mechanism: A source sends packets at a nominal fixed interval (incT) from a randomly chosen start time T0 until a stop time Tf, and delay, delay variation and loss are computed from time stamps taken at measurement points near the source and destination.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines the Type-P-One-way-Delay-Periodic-Stream metric, how to account for clock, host and interval errors, what to report, and the security risks of abuse and interference.

today: RFC 3432 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the framework in RFC 2330 and the one-way delay metric in RFC 2679.

sections.title: Why Sample Periodically
sections.content:
RFC 3432 describes a sampling method and metrics for IP network performance. The original driver was the quality of interactive periodic streams such as multimedia conferencing. Sending equally sized (or mostly same-size) packets at regular intervals simulates a constant bit-rate (CBR) or nearly CBR stream, and the memo calls such traffic a periodic stream.

The IPPM framework in RFC 2330 notes that regularly spaced tests sample only part of the network performance spectrum. The memo argues that periodic sampling is still useful: it works for passive as well as active measurement, an active test can match the characteristics of media flows, impairments such as delay variation, consecutive loss and reordering are sensitive to sampling frequency, and equally spaced samples simplify frequency-domain analysis.

Typical multimedia flows have 10 to 100 packets in each second, so this kind of sampling is dense and can capture short-lived network phenomena. The goal is comparable results from independent implementations, which is why the key words of RFC 2119 are used to mark where implementations must agree.
sections.eli5: Video calls send little packets at a steady beat, like a drum. To test the network the way a call would use it, you send test packets with the same steady beat.

sections.title: The Periodic Sampling Method
sections.content:
The framework warns of two problems with periodic sampling. The results may line up with some other periodic behaviour, or someone may predict the samples and manipulate the results. Also, active measurement can cause congestion and could push congestion-aware senders into a synchronized state. Poisson sampling gives an unbiased sample, but periodic sampling is better in the situations listed in the motivation.

The memo reduces predictability by using random start times and limited stream duration. Five configuration parameters define a sample: T, the start of the interval in which a sample is wanted; dT, the length of the interval of allowed start times; T0, which MUST be chosen at random from [T, T+dT]; Tf, the stop time; and incT, the nominal first-bit-to-first-bit gap between packets.

T0 may be drawn from a uniform distribution, and start times in successive intervals MUST use an independent value. In passive measurement, the arrival of user media flows may be random enough, or a randomized start during a flow may be needed. The total test traffic should be limited so it does not harm other traffic, taking packet size, rate, sample duration and frequency into account.
sections.eli5: The test starts at a surprise moment so nobody can guess when it is coming, and it stops after a while so it does not clog the road. In between, the cars leave at an even pace.

sections.title: Metric Parameters
sections.content:
The metric is named Type-P-One-way-Delay-Periodic-Stream and is similar to the Poisson-stream metric of RFC 2679. Global parameters include the source and destination addresses (Src, Dst), the IP version, dTloss (the longest a packet may take before it counts as lost) and the packet size p(j). Optional ones are PktType and Tcons, the time for consolidating data from the measurement points.

Two measurement points, MP(Src) and MP(Dst), each record a time stamp per packet. They also record a unique packet ID or sequence number and the actual packet size. At the destination side, optional values are dTstop (extra time after Tf to keep collecting) and PktStatus, which can be OK, header corrupt, payload corrupt, duplicate or fragment. If a status is used, the criteria MUST be specified.

The RFC assumes a topology where Src and Dst are separate from the measurement points.
sections.eli5: Two referees stand by the road, one at the start and one at the finish. Each writes down which car passed and when, and a car that never shows up in time is counted as lost.

sections.title: Collecting a Sample and Computing Delay
sections.content:
Beginning on or after T0, Src sends Type-P packets to Dst until Tf, with nominal interval incT between the first bits of successive packets. The interval is only nominal because of variation in packet generation and clock issues. MP(Src) records packets stamped between T0 and Tf. MP(Dst) records until Tf plus dTstop. Optionally at Tf + Tcons, and eventually in all cases, the data from both points are consolidated. dTcons should be at least dTstop, and dTstop should be a reasonable time even if dTloss is infinite.

Per-packet delay is Delay[i] = Tstamp(Dst)[i] - Tstamp(Src)[i]. No delay can be computed for spurious packets (no source time stamp), packets not received, or packets with corrupt headers. For duplicates, only the first non-corrupt copy gets a delay. A sample average is AveDelay = (1/N) Sum Delay[i]. Delay variation is IPDV[i] = Delay[i] - Delay[i-1], which may be negative, zero or positive and is undefined unless both delays can be calculated. An example summary is RangeIPDV = max(IPDV[]) - min(IPDV[]).

The memo also gives guidance: the test should be long enough to represent real use but not excessive, the packet rate should not exceed the capacity of the ports or network, and delays above dTloss are treated as loss. Synchronizing the two clocks matters, since delays may be as low as 100 usec to 10 msec. GPS can reach several tens of usec, while ordinary NTP may reach only several msec.
sections.eli5: For each car, subtract the start time from the finish time to get its trip time. If the trip times keep changing, that wobble is the delay variation.

sections.title: Errors, Calibration and Reporting
sections.content:
Any implementation should account for three error sources: variation of incT (for example uneven process scheduling), uncertainty in the source and destination clocks, and the gap between wire time and host time. Clock error covers synchronization error (Tsynch), clock resolution and skew. The total clock-related uncertainty is Esynch(t) + Rsource + Rdest, and the wire-versus-host uncertainty is Hsource + Hdest. For incT, the RFC notes that H.323 systems are required to have packets ready within 5 ms of their ideal time.

Calibration splits a measured value into true value, systematic error and random error. Systematic error should be removed if known. At minimum, a bound e should be found so the reported value is within true value plus or minus e at least 95 percent of the time. One suggested method connects two instruments back to back, repeats the test at least hundreds of times, takes the median as the systematic error, and uses the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the deviations. Calibration should use the same measurement load as in the field.

Reporting is strict. The exact Type-P and the threshold for delay equivalent to loss MUST be reported. The calibration error SHOULD be reported, and so SHOULD the path, if possible, and background conditions. The RFC notes that recording the route is often impractical because many routers do not support it and it can worsen the observed performance.
sections.eli5: A stopwatch can be a little off, and the person pressing it can be a little slow. Good testers check how wrong their stopwatch usually is and tell you, so you know how much to trust the numbers.

sections.title: Using the Method in Practice
sections.content:
Applications react differently to lost packets, long delays, duplicates, reordering, corrupt headers or payloads, and spurious packets. For example, most applications treat a corrupt header like a loss, while some voice codecs accept a corrupt payload. Operators may want to keep these cases distinct.

The reference setup puts MP(Src) close to where packets leave Src and MP(Dst) close to where they enter Dst, so results match a direct Src-to-Dst measurement within the error target (the RFC gives under 1 ms as an example). Three delay measurement styles are described: one-way, paired one-way and round-trip. Paired one-way catches asymmetry: the RFC's example has 30ms one way and 120ms the other, which a round-trip average of 150ms would hide even though one direction averages more than 100ms.

The RFC also works through an example of 100 packets, in which 80 arrive within 20 ms and intact, so 80 percent are acceptable. An application that tolerates corrupt payloads and any delay would count (80+8+3)/100 = 91 percent. Multiple samples can form a "sample of samples", such as 1,000 two-minute VoIP calls instead of one 2,000 minute call.
sections.eli5: It is better to time each direction of a trip separately. If you go to school in 30 minutes but come home in 120, only the one-way timings reveal the slow trip.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method sends a periodic packet stream from one host to another and could be abused for denial of service against the destination or the networks in between. Administrators of the source, destination and intervening networks should agree on the timing, size and frequency of samples. Use beyond what was agreed may justify immediate rejection, discarding of packets or other escalation.

Active use generates its own packets and does not threaten user data confidentiality. Passive measurement must restrict attention to the headers of interest, and since payloads may be temporarily stored for length analysis, suitable precautions MUST be taken to keep them safe and confidential.

Someone who can recognize test packets could treat them differently and distort the results, or inject extra packets that look like part of the sample. To discourage this, packet interference checks such as a cryptographic hash MAY be used. The RFC has no IANA considerations because it defines no protocol or well-known values.
sections.eli5: A flood of test packets can annoy the receiver like a stream of knocks on the door, so people should agree beforehand. And nobody should sneak in fake test cars to fool the count.

items.desc: Duration of the interval for allowed sample start times.

items.desc: Chosen at random from [T, T+dT]; packets start here.

items.desc: Time, greater than T0, for stopping packet generation.
